title: API & Interface Design
description: Designing intuitive, foolproof, and stable C++ public interfaces, contracts, preconditions, and ABI evolution.

topics.title: Designing Intuitive & Hard-to-Misuse Interfaces
topics.description: Scott Meyers' rule: 'Make interfaces easy to use correctly and hard to use incorrectly.'

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: A well-designed public interface uses strong typing, [[nodiscard]], explicit constructors, and const-correctness to prevent caller misuse at compile time.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Stringly-typed APIs (e.g. setTime(int, int, int) where caller mixes up hours, minutes, and seconds) cause catastrophic production bugs.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Use Strong Types (e.g. Seconds, Milliseconds) instead of raw integers.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Design APIs where invalid states fail to compile.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Strong Typing Defense
callout.text: Before: setDuration(1000); // Is it seconds or milliseconds?\nAfter: setDuration(std::chrono::milliseconds(1000)); // Completely unambiguous!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Strong types UserId and OrderId prevent parameter ordering bugs at compile time.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Chrono duration types, Financial currency APIs, Embedded GPIO pin configurations.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use strong types whenever an interface accepts multiple parameters of the same primitive type.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not create wrappers for trivial single-argument helper functions.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Eliminates subtle parameter swapping bugs at compile time.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Small amount of boilerplate wrapper struct definitions.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Strong Typedefs, Enum Classes, Chrono Durations, Named Parameters.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Accepting boolean flags (e.g. initialize(true, false, true)) instead of explicit enum options.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why is setMode(bool isFast, bool isEncrypted) a bad interface design?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Because call sites look like setMode(true, false), which is completely unreadable and prone to swapping argument order. An enum class (setMode(Speed::FAST, Security::ENCRYPTED)) is self-documenting and foolproof.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Create strong types Latitude and Longitude to prevent coordinate swapping.

practice.title: Strong Type Coordinates
practice.problemStatement: Create strong types Latitude and Longitude to prevent coordinate swapping.

referenceCode.code: struct Latitude { double val; }; struct Longitude { double val; };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Designing Intuitive & Hard-to-Misuse Interfaces is essential for advanced C++ systems design.

topics.title: Design by Contract (Preconditions, Postconditions, Invariants)
topics.description: Formalizing software correctness through preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content:
Design by Contract (DbC) views software components as collaborating parties fulfilling mutual obligations:
• Preconditions: What must be true before calling a method.
• Postconditions: What the method guarantees upon return.
• Invariants: What must remain true throughout object lifetime.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Unclear contracts lead to defensive code duplication where every function re-validates the same inputs.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: If the caller violates preconditions, the method fails fast (assert / throw). The method guarantees postconditions.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Use assert() for programming bugs and exceptions for runtime environment failures.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Contract Triad
callout.text:
Precondition: balance >= amount
Action: balance -= amount
Postcondition: balance == old_balance - amount
Invariant: balance >= overdraft_limit

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: BoundedBuffer validates preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Mission-critical avionics (Eiffel, Ada), safety-critical automotive systems (AUTOSAR C++).

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use DbC thinking in all domain classes to clarify caller vs callee obligations.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not disable precondition checks in production without verified static analysis.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Self-documenting, mathematically verifiable system integrity.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Adds assertion overhead during debug builds.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: C++20/26 Contracts, Assertions, Static Analysis annotations.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Treating precondition bugs as catchable runtime exceptions instead of fixing the caller bug.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the difference between a Precondition violation and a Runtime Exception?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: A Precondition violation is a bug in the calling code (should never happen in correct software). A Runtime Exception is an unpredictable environmental failure (e.g. disk full, network lost).

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement pop() verifying precondition !empty() and postcondition size == old - 1.

practice.title: Stack Contract Verification
practice.problemStatement: Implement pop() verifying precondition !empty() and postcondition size == old - 1.

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Design by Contract (Preconditions, Postconditions, Invariants) is essential for advanced C++ systems design.

topics.title: API Evolution, Versioning & Extensibility
topics.description: Evolving C++ APIs without breaking existing clients or binary ABI compatibility.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Techniques for evolving C++ libraries gracefully: Deprecation attributes ([[deprecated]]), default arguments, versioned inline namespaces, and PImpl ABI preservation.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Breaking changes in public APIs force all dependent client projects to rewrite code and recompile.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Never remove or change existing function signatures in minor versions; add overloaded extensions and mark old methods deprecated.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Use inline namespace v2 to version APIs seamlessly.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Inline Namespace Versioning
callout.text: namespace Lib { inline namespace v2 { class Engine; } namespace v1 { class Engine; } }

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Demonstrates seamless API evolution using inline namespace v2 and [[deprecated]] attributes.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Boost C++ libraries, Standard Library versioning, Game engine SDKs.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when publishing reusable libraries used by other development teams.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not over-engineer versioning for internal single-team applications.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Smooth deprecation cycles without abrupt breaking changes.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Maintaining legacy version code increases library footprint.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Inline Namespaces, SemVer, Deprecation Warnings, PImpl ABI firewalls.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Modifying the memory layout of exported classes in minor version library updates (breaking ABI).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How do inline namespaces enable library versioning in C++11?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: An inline namespace makes its members accessible in the enclosing namespace without qualification by default, allowing new versions to be default while keeping older version namespaces explicitly available.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Mark old login() method [[deprecated]] while providing modern login(token).

practice.title: Deprecated Method Migration
practice.problemStatement: Mark old login() method [[deprecated]] while providing modern login(token).

referenceCode.code: class Auth { public: [[deprecated]] void login(string u, string p); void login(Token t); };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering API Evolution, Versioning & Extensibility is essential for advanced C++ systems design.
